title: Tree
body:
[[Binary Search Tree]]
[[Balanced Tree]]

A hierarchical [[Data Structure]]: a root node, each node holding references to its
children, and no cycles anywhere. Every node except the root has exactly one parent, so
there is exactly one path from the root to any node. That is what separates a tree from a
[[Graph]]: a tree is a connected graph with no cycles.

```
        root
       /    \
   inner    inner
   /  \        \
 leaf leaf    leaf        height = 2 (edges on the longest root-to-leaf path)
```

## Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Root | the one node with no parent |
| Leaf | a node with no children |
| Height | edges on the longest root-to-leaf path |
| Depth | edges from the root down to a given node |
| Subtree | any node plus everything below it, which is itself a tree |
| Binary tree | at most two children per node |
| Complete | every level full except the last, which fills left to right |

The subtree line is the important one. Because a subtree is a tree, almost every tree
algorithm is written with [[Recursion]]: handle the node, then call yourself on each child,
with the empty tree as the base case.

## Why they matter

Height is the whole story on cost. A binary tree of $n$ nodes has height as low as
$\log_2 n$ when it is bushy and as high as $n - 1$ when it is a chain, and every operation
that walks from root to leaf costs the height. So a [[Binary Search Tree]] gives
$O(\log n)$ search *while it stays bushy*, degenerates into a [[Linked List]] when it does
not, and a [[Balanced Tree]] exists purely to stop that happening. A [[Heap]] is a third
discipline again: a complete tree with a weaker ordering rule, packed into an [[Array]].

Trees are everywhere outside this course too: the [[Directory]] hierarchy in
[[OPERATING SYSTEMS]], the parse tree a compiler builds, the [[DOM]] a browser builds, the
[[Inheritance]] hierarchy of a class design, decision trees in [[MACHINE LEARNING]].
